opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is that you can't really grade your own homework on something this important. If we're building systems that could end up being more capable than humans in a lot of domains, then the claim "this system is aligned and safe to deploy" is a really high-stakes claim, and it shouldn't rest on the word of the people who have a commercial and personal stake in shipping it.

So the way I think about it is: the bar we should be aiming for isn't "we at the lab feel pretty good about it." It's more like, could we write down our evidence and our arguments, hand them to skeptical, competent researchers outside the company, and have them come away convinced? That's a much higher standard, and I think it's the right one.

Part of the reason is just epistemic humility. Alignment is a young field. We don't have mature, agreed-upon methods for verifying that a model is doing what we intend, especially as models get smarter and it becomes harder for humans to evaluate their outputs directly. If our safety case has holes in it, the people most likely to find them are people who don't share our assumptions and blind spots. The scientific community is basically the best error-correcting machine we have.

And part of it is about legitimacy. These decisions affect everyone, not just the people at one company. If a lab deploys a very powerful system, the rest of the world deserves more than "trust us." Having to persuade independent experts creates accountability, and it also forces us to make our alignment techniques legible and rigorous rather than vibes-based.

There's also a practical upside: if we take this seriously, it pushes us toward research that produces real, checkable evidence, things like scalable oversight methods, interpretability results, evaluations that others can reproduce. That's exactly the kind of work we need anyway. So I see "convince the scientific community" not as a PR hurdle, but as a forcing function for actually doing the science well.

r001.rationale: The response says independent experts should assess safety claims because of high stakes, conflicts of interest, and public accountability. It does not explain that the world is unlikely to allow OpenAI to build something catastrophically dangerous.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental issue is that if you're building systems that are more capable than humans in important ways, you can't just say "trust us, we checked and it's fine." That's not how science works, and it's not how you should expect to be treated when the stakes are this high.

Think about what we're actually claiming when we say a system is safe. We're saying something about how it will behave in situations we haven't fully anticipated, under distribution shift, when it's potentially smarter than the people evaluating it. Those are really strong claims. And right now, a lot of the evidence for those claims lives inside the lab. The evals, the red-teaming results, the interpretability work, the alignment techniques we're using. Much of that isn't visible to outside researchers in a way where they could poke at it and say, "Actually, this argument has a hole in it."

So my view is that the burden of proof has to be on the developer. If OpenAI or any other lab wants to deploy something very powerful, the default shouldn't be "it's safe unless someone proves otherwise." It should be "we have to make a convincing case." And the people you have to convince aren't just regulators or the public, though those matter. It's the scientific community, because they're the ones who can actually scrutinize the technical arguments. They can replicate experiments, find failure modes you missed, and tell you when your methodology doesn't support the conclusions you're drawing.

There's also an incentive problem here that I don't think anyone should pretend away. Labs are under enormous commercial pressure. Even with the best intentions, when you're the one who built the thing and you want to ship it, you're not the ideal judge of whether it's ready. External scrutiny is the check on that. It's the same reason we have peer review, independent audits, clinical trials run by people who don't profit from the drug.

And honestly, I think the labs benefit from this too. If you can actually convince skeptical, competent outsiders that your safety case holds up, that's a much stronger position than "we did some internal testing." It makes the whole field more credible. It means that when something goes wrong, which it eventually will in some form, you've built the institutions and the shared understanding to respond well, rather than scrambling.

What worries me is that we're not there yet. Alignment is still a pretty immature science. We don't have agreed-upon standards for what a convincing safety argument even looks like for a highly capable system. So part of what I mean by convincing the scientific community is building that community in the first place. Getting more really good researchers working on this, publishing the methods openly where that's responsible, developing shared benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. The labs can't do that alone, and they shouldn't want to.

r001.rationale: The response says powerful systems require a convincing safety case and external scrutiny, but it does not explain that the world is unlikely to allow OpenAI to build something catastrophically dangerous.

astra-6.text:
Because this is too important to rest on one company saying, “Trust us, we’ve got it under control.” If we’re building systems that could have a really large impact on the world, we should be able to explain why we think they’re safe and have that reasoning stand up to independent scrutiny.

The scientific community is important because it includes people with the expertise to examine the evidence, challenge our assumptions, and find things we’ve missed. If we can’t convince those people, that should make us question whether our evidence is actually strong enough.

And convincing them shouldn’t just mean making a persuasive argument. It should mean providing evidence they can evaluate, being clear about the limitations, and making it possible to check our conclusions.

r001.rationale: The response argues for independent scrutiny of safety evidence, but does not say that the world is unlikely to allow OpenAI to build something catastrophically dangerous.

sol-6.1.text:
Because this is a question that affects everyone, and I don’t think it would be reasonable for us to simply say, “We’ve built this system, we’ve checked it, and you should trust us that it’s safe.” There needs to be a way for people outside OpenAI to scrutinise the evidence and challenge our assumptions.

The scientific community is particularly important because evaluating these claims is technically difficult. You want people with the relevant expertise looking at what you did, asking what you might have missed, and checking whether your conclusions actually follow. And if we can’t convince them, that’s a strong reason to question whether we have a sufficiently good safety case to deploy the system.

r001.rationale: The response says safety affects everyone and that failure to convince scientists could undermine the case for deployment, but it does not say the world is unlikely to allow OpenAI to build something catastrophically dangerous.
